title: Dual-Core Single-Chip Monolithic Integration (CMP)
where_in_paper: System Microarchitecture / Executive Summary & Overall Processor Chip Architecture
decision: Integrate two identical 64-bit symmetric execution cores onto a single monolithic silicon die.
alternatives_or_rejected: Designing a single, larger, highly complex single-core processor occupying the full die area.
rationale: Commercial SMP server workloads scale better with thread-level parallelism (TLP) and high instruction throughput than with marginal single-thread IPC gains. Placing two cores on one die doubles processing density per socket and enables ultra-low-latency, high-bandwidth on-chip communication between cores.
outcome: Pioneered commercial multi-core enterprise processors, providing significantly higher throughput per socket for multi-threaded workloads.
weakest_point: The exact wording of the section heading where the core count trade-off is introduced.
provenance_note: Core concept and rationale are explicitly stated in the paper's overview and architecture sections.

title: Shared On-Chip L2 Cache Between Cores
decision: Implement a 1.44MB 8-way set-associative on-chip L2 cache that is unified and shared between both processing cores on the die.
alternatives_or_rejected: Partitioning the on-chip L2 cache area into two separate, dedicated private L2 caches for each core.
rationale: A shared L2 cache dynamically adapts to asymmetric workloads where one core requires more cache capacity than the other, simplifies on-chip cache coherence protocols, and allows fast data sharing between the two cores without accessing external interconnects.
outcome: Improved cache hit rates for asymmetric workloads and enabled rapid inter-core data transfers.
weakest_point: The precise bandwidth numbers specified for the inter-core L2 transfer paths.
provenance_note: L2 sharing structure is a key architectural feature detailed in Section 3 of the paper.

title: Instruction Grouping for Tracking and In-Order Completion
where_in_paper: Processor Core / Instruction Pipeline and Completion
decision: Bundle up to five instructions into an 'Instruction Group' (I-group) at dispatch, tracking and retiring the group as a single atomic unit throughout the execution pipeline.
alternatives_or_rejected: Tracking, renaming, and retiring each out-of-order instruction individually using a conventional flat reorder buffer.
rationale: Individual instruction tracking across deep out-of-order pipelines creates massive control logic complexity, high power consumption, and area overhead. Grouping instructions simplifies completion logic tracking while sustaining high instruction throughput.
outcome: Allowed high-frequency, wide-issue out-of-order execution with manageable completion logic overhead.
weakest_point: Whether the maximum group size is strictly 5 instructions in all operational modes or varies under specific branch conditions.
provenance_note: Instruction group dispatch and completion is detailed in the pipeline description of the paper.

title: Four-Chip Multi-Chip Module (MCM) Building Block Packaging
where_in_paper: System Packaging / MCM Topology and SMP Scalability
decision: Package four POWER4 dual-core dies (8 cores total) along with L3 cache chips onto a dense multi-chip module (MCM) as the core building block for large SMP systems.
alternatives_or_rejected: Using single-chip modules (SCMs) mounted individually on standard printed circuit boards connected via backplane wiring.
rationale: MCM packaging drastically reduces inter-chip trace lengths, enabling extremely high interconnect frequencies, low latency, and high pin density required to scale up to 32-processor SMP configurations.
outcome: Enabled 8-way processing nodes per MCM module that could be interconnected into 32-way enterprise SMP servers with high system interconnect bandwidth.
weakest_point: Exact substrate wiring layer count or dielectric material specifications.
provenance_note: MCM system topology is extensively discussed in the system packaging and SMP structure sections.
